topics.name: Checks and balances
topics.kicker: Each branch can limit the other two · Built into the U.S. Constitution
topics.briefing: What keeps a president from acting like a king? The Constitution splits power among three branches and then gives each one ways to rein in the other two. The president can veto bills, Congress can override vetoes and impeach officials, and the courts can strike down laws. James Madison explained this system of checks and balances in _Federalist_ No. 51: “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.”
topics.answerHtml: checks and balances (accept system of checks and balances; prompt on separation of powers; do not accept “federalism”)
accept: a system of checks and balances
the system of checks and balances

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a 1748 book, the French writer Montesquieu [“MON-tes-kyoo”] warned that liberty is lost when one person or group holds the powers to make the laws, to carry them out, and to judge. He praised the government of Great Britain for dividing power so that each part could restrain the others.
tossups.r: That book was _The Spirit of the Laws_. For 10 points, name this system, built into the U.S. Constitution, that lets each branch of government limit the other two.

tossups.p: One essay argued that “ambition must be made to counteract ambition” and that each branch of government needs the “personal motives to resist” the others. The same essay, _Federalist_ No. 51, famously says that “if men were angels, no government would be necessary.”
tossups.r: Its author, James Madison, was explaining this idea. For 10 points, name this system in which each branch of government can limit the powers of the others.

tossups.p: In 1845, John Tyler became the first president to have Congress overturn one of his rejections of a bill, on a bill about ships called revenue cutters. Two decades later, Congress overturned Andrew Johnson’s rejection of the Civil Rights Act of 1866, the first major law ever passed that way.
tossups.r: Overriding a veto takes two-thirds of each house. For 10 points, name this system that lets each branch of government limit the other two.

tossups.p: In an 1803 case brought by William Marbury against James Madison, Chief Justice John Marshall declared that it is “emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” That decision gave the courts a powerful new tool under this principle.
tossups.r: That tool, judicial review, lets courts strike down laws that break the Constitution. For 10 points, name this system in which each branch of government can limit the others.

tossups.p: In 1987, the Senate voted 58 to 42 against Robert Bork, Ronald Reagan’s nominee for the Supreme Court. That vote showed this principle at work, because the Constitution requires the Senate’s “advice and consent” before judges and other top officials can take office.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system that keeps any one branch of government from becoming too powerful.

tossups.p: Senator Henry Cabot Lodge led the opposition that kept the Senate from approving the Treaty of Versailles, which Woodrow Wilson had helped write after World War I. That defeat showed this principle at work, since a treaty needs the votes of two-thirds of the senators present.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system that lets each branch of the U.S. government limit the powers of the others.

tossups.p: Chief Justice Salmon Chase presided in 1868 when the Senate fell one vote short of the two-thirds it needed to remove President Andrew Johnson from office. Johnson had angered Congress by trying to fire his Secretary of War, Edwin Stanton.
tossups.r: The power to impeach and remove officials is one tool of this principle. For 10 points, name this system in which each branch of government can limit the others.

tossups.p: After the Supreme Court struck down several New Deal laws, Franklin Roosevelt proposed in 1937 to add up to six new justices, but Congress refused to pass his plan. Critics called it a “court-packing” plan and said it threatened the independence of the courts and this principle.
tossups.r: The president’s veto is another part of this idea. For 10 points, name this system that lets each branch of government limit the other two.

tossups.p: In 1974, the Supreme Court ruled 8–0 that Richard Nixon had to hand over his secret Watergate tapes, rejecting his claim of executive privilege. That decision in _United States v. Nixon_ showed the courts using this principle to limit the president.
tossups.r: Nixon resigned about two weeks later. For 10 points, name this system in which each branch of government can limit the powers of the others.

tossups.p: The Greek historian Polybius [“puh-LIB-ee-us”] praised the government of the Roman Republic because its consuls, its Senate, and its popular assemblies could each hold back the others. Many centuries later, the framers of the U.S. Constitution built a version of that idea into their plan.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system, which includes the president’s veto and the courts’ power to strike down laws.

tossups.p: The Eleventh Amendment, ratified in 1795, reversed the Supreme Court’s ruling in _Chisholm v. Georgia_ [“CHIZ-um”], and the Sixteenth Amendment allowed a federal income tax after the Court had struck one down in 1895. Those amendments show how Congress and the states can overrule the courts under this principle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system in which the branches of government can limit one another.

tossups.p: Passed over Richard Nixon’s veto in 1973, the War Powers Resolution requires the president to notify Congress within 48 hours of sending troops into combat. Congress’s powers to declare war and to control spending, often called the “power of the purse,” are also tools of this principle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system that keeps any one branch of government from growing too strong.

tossups.p: In _Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer_, the Supreme Court ruled in 1952 that Harry Truman could not take over the nation’s steel mills during the Korean War without approval from Congress. That decision is a famous example of this principle limiting a president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system in which each branch of government can limit the powers of the other two.

tossups.p: John Adams’s 1776 pamphlet _Thoughts on Government_ urged Americans writing new state constitutions to create a two-house legislature, a separate executive, and independent judges, so that each part could restrain the others. About a decade later, the framers of the Constitution built that design into the national government.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system, under which the president can veto bills and Congress can override vetoes.

tossups.p: In 1989, the Senate voted 53 to 47 to reject John Tower, George H. W. Bush’s choice to be Secretary of Defense. The Constitution requires the Senate to approve Cabinet members, ambassadors, and federal judges, which is one way this principle limits a president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system that lets each branch of government limit the others.

clues.t: The system that lets each branch of government limit the powers of the other two, so that no branch grows too strong
The president can veto bills; Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses
Judicial review: courts can strike down laws that break the Constitution
The House can impeach officials, and the Senate can remove them with a two-thirds vote
Works together with the separation of powers among the legislative, executive, and judicial branches (Articles I, II, and III)
_Federalist_ No. 51 (James Madison): “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition”; “If men were angels, no government would be necessary”
Montesquieu’s _The Spirit of the Laws_ (1748) warned against letting one person or group make, enforce, and judge the laws
_Marbury v. Madison_ (1803): John Marshall said it is the courts’ duty “to say what the law is”
“Advice and consent”: the Senate must approve federal judges, Cabinet members, and ambassadors
Treaties need the votes of two-thirds of the senators present; the Senate refused to approve the Treaty of Versailles (1919–1920)
_United States v. Nixon_ (1974): the Supreme Court ruled 8–0 that Nixon had to hand over the Watergate tapes, rejecting executive privilege
Franklin Roosevelt’s 1937 “court-packing” plan to add up to six justices failed in Congress
Congress controls spending (the “power of the purse”) and has the power to declare war
In 1868, the Senate fell one vote short of removing Andrew Johnson; the Chief Justice presides when a president is tried
The Greek historian Polybius praised the Roman Republic, whose consuls, Senate, and assemblies could each hold back the others
Montesquieu admired Great Britain’s government for dividing power so each part could restrain the others; _Federalist_ No. 47 calls him “the oracle”
Congress first overrode a veto in 1845, against John Tyler, on a bill about revenue cutters
The Civil Rights Act of 1866 was the first major law passed over a veto; Congress overrode Andrew Johnson a record 15 times
In 1987, the Senate rejected Robert Bork, Ronald Reagan’s Supreme Court nominee, by a vote of 58 to 42
In 1989, the Senate rejected John Tower, George H. W. Bush’s choice for Secretary of Defense, by 53 to 47
Senator Henry Cabot Lodge led the opposition to Woodrow Wilson’s Treaty of Versailles
_Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer_ (1952): Truman could not seize the steel mills during the Korean War without Congress’s approval
War Powers Resolution (1973), passed over Nixon’s veto: Congress must be told within 48 hours when troops go into combat
Amendments can reverse court rulings: the 11th Amendment (1795) reversed _Chisholm v. Georgia_; the 16th allowed an income tax after an 1895 ruling
John Adams’s _Thoughts on Government_ (1776) called for a two-house legislature, a separate executive, and independent judges
Andrew Johnson was impeached after trying to fire Secretary of War Edwin Stanton; Chief Justice Salmon Chase presided at his trial

trap.title: Checks or separation?
trap.body: Two answer lines share almost every clue. The separation of powers means dividing the government into three branches with different jobs; checks and balances means giving each branch tools to limit the others, like the veto, the override, impeachment, and judicial review. Saying “separation of powers” may earn only a prompt, and “federalism,” which divides power between the national and state governments, is wrong.
trap.fix: If the clue shows one branch blocking, overruling, or approving another, say “checks and balances.” If it is only about splitting jobs among branches, think separation of powers; if it is about the states versus the national government, think federalism.
trap.line: Real answer line: checks and balances (prompt on separation of powers; do not accept “federalism”)

topics.name: Compromise of 1850
topics.kicker: Henry Clay’s last great deal · Admitted California as a free state
topics.briefing: By 1849, the gold rush had brought so many settlers to California that it asked to become a state, with a constitution that banned slavery. Southern leaders warned they might leave the Union. Henry Clay offered a package deal, and after months of fierce debate, Stephen Douglas pushed it through Congress as five separate laws. The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state but also created a harsh new Fugitive Slave Act.
topics.answerHtml: Compromise of 1850 (prompt on compromise alone or Omnibus Bill; do not accept “Missouri Compromise,” “Kansas–Nebraska Act,” “Fugitive Slave Act,” or “Compromise of 1877”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Senator James Mason of Virginia read aloud the last major speech of a dying John C. Calhoun, who opposed this plan and warned that the Union could break apart. Calhoun died less than a month later, about half a year before Congress finally passed this plan.
tossups.r: Henry Clay had proposed it. For 10 points, name this group of laws that admitted California to the Union as a free state.

tossups.p: “I wish to speak today, not as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Northern man, but as an American,” began a Seventh of March speech in favor of this plan. That speech by Daniel Webster angered many abolitionists, and John Greenleaf Whittier attacked him in the poem “Ichabod.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of laws, proposed by Henry Clay, that included a tougher Fugitive Slave Act.

tossups.p: William Seward of New York opposed this plan in a Senate speech claiming that there is “a higher law than the Constitution.” Seward argued that slavery should not be allowed to spread into the lands the United States had won in the war with Mexico.
tossups.r: Millard Fillmore signed this plan’s laws after Zachary Taylor’s death. For 10 points, name this set of laws that admitted California as a free state.

tossups.p: A president who had been a hero of the war with Mexico opposed this plan, but he died after falling ill following a Fourth of July celebration. His successor, a New Yorker, supported this plan and signed each of its laws that September.
tossups.r: Those presidents were Zachary Taylor and Millard Fillmore. For 10 points, name this set of laws, proposed by Henry Clay, that admitted California as a free state.

tossups.p: During the Senate debate over this plan, Henry Foote of Mississippi pulled a pistol on Thomas Hart Benton of Missouri, though no shot was fired. Months later, this plan passed only after it was broken up into separate bills.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this set of laws, proposed by Henry Clay, that admitted California as a free state and banned the slave trade in Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: A Senate committee of thirteen bundled the parts of this plan into a single “Omnibus Bill,” which opponents picked apart in July. Illinois senator Stephen Douglas then split that bill into separate measures and steered each one through Congress.
tossups.r: This plan’s author was Henry Clay of Kentucky. For 10 points, name this set of laws that admitted California as a free state.

tossups.p: Under this plan, Texas gave up its claims to land in present-day New Mexico, and the federal government agreed to pay ten million dollars toward Texas’s old debts. The same plan organized the territories of New Mexico and Utah without banning slavery in them.
tossups.r: Settlers there would decide the question by popular sovereignty. For 10 points, name this set of laws that admitted California as a free state.

tossups.p: This plan ended the buying and selling of enslaved people in Washington, D.C., though slavery itself stayed legal in the capital until 1862. Antislavery leaders had long protested that human beings were sold at markets in the nation’s capital.
tossups.r: This plan also admitted California as a free state. For 10 points, name this set of laws proposed by Henry Clay.

tossups.p: This plan let the settlers of the Utah and New Mexico territories decide for themselves whether to allow slavery, an idea called popular sovereignty. Four years later, Stephen Douglas used the same idea in the Kansas–Nebraska Act, which repealed the 36°30′ line drawn in 1820.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this set of laws, proposed by Henry Clay, that admitted California as a free state.

tossups.p: Before this plan passed, the Senate was evenly split between fifteen free states and fifteen slave states, and Southern senators feared that adding one more free state would give the North a lasting majority. That fear set off the long debate that produced this plan.
tossups.r: This plan admitted California as a free state. For 10 points, name this set of laws proposed by Henry Clay.

tossups.p: This plan tried to settle a fight that began in 1846, when Pennsylvania congressman David Wilmot proposed banning slavery from all land won in the war with Mexico. Wilmot’s idea passed the House of Representatives but never passed the Senate.
tossups.r: This plan instead let settlers in Utah and New Mexico decide on slavery. For 10 points, name this group of laws that admitted California as a free state.

tossups.p: While Congress debated this plan, delegates from several slave states met at the Nashville Convention to discuss how to defend slavery in the West, and some of them called for leaving the Union. Months later, this plan calmed the crisis, at least for a time.
tossups.r: Its laws were signed by Millard Fillmore. For 10 points, name this set of laws that admitted California as a free state.

tossups.p: One part of this plan paid federal commissioners ten dollars for sending an accused person south into slavery but only five dollars for setting the person free. That part helped inspire Harriet Beecher Stowe to write _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_.
tossups.r: That part was the Fugitive Slave Act. For 10 points, name this set of five laws that also admitted California as a free state.

tossups.p: This plan was the last of three famous deals between North and South worked out by one statesman, after a tariff deal in 1833 and an 1820 agreement over the admission of Maine and Missouri. That statesman died in 1852, two years after this plan passed.
tossups.r: That statesman was Henry Clay. For 10 points, name this set of laws that admitted California as a free state.

tossups.p: This plan set off the last great Senate debate among the three members of the “Great Triumvirate.” Daniel Webster supported this plan, John C. Calhoun opposed it, and the third member of that trio had proposed it.
tossups.r: That third member was Henry Clay. For 10 points, name this group of laws that admitted California as a free state and created a stricter Fugitive Slave Act.

clues.t: Admitted California to the Union as a free state (the 31st state)
Proposed by Henry Clay, a Whig senator from Kentucky
Included a tougher Fugitive Slave Act, which forced free states to help return people who had escaped slavery
Signed by President Millard Fillmore in September, about two months after he took office
Banned the slave trade (but not slavery itself) in Washington, D.C.
Organized the Utah and New Mexico territories, letting settlers decide on slavery by popular sovereignty
Stephen Douglas passed it as separate bills after Clay’s “Omnibus Bill” fell apart in July
President Zachary Taylor opposed it but died in July; his successor, Millard Fillmore, supported it
Daniel Webster backed it in his Seventh of March speech: “not as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Northern man, but as an American”
A dying John C. Calhoun’s last major speech, against it, was read aloud in March by Senator James Mason of Virginia
Texas gave up land claims in present-day New Mexico in exchange for $10 million toward its old debts
California’s admission broke the Senate’s even split of 15 free states and 15 slave states
Settled, for a time, the fight over slavery in the land won from Mexico in 1848 (the Mexican Cession)
William Seward of New York opposed it, saying there is “a higher law than the Constitution”
During the debate, Henry Foote of Mississippi pulled a pistol on Thomas Hart Benton of Missouri on the Senate floor in April
A Senate Committee of Thirteen, chaired by Clay, bundled its parts into one “Omnibus Bill”
John Greenleaf Whittier attacked Webster for supporting it in the poem “Ichabod”
Slavery itself stayed legal in Washington, D.C., until 1862
The fight began with the Wilmot Proviso (1846), which tried to ban slavery in land won from Mexico; it passed the House but not the Senate
While it was debated, delegates from several slave states met at the Nashville Convention, and some called for leaving the Union
Its Fugitive Slave Act paid commissioners $10 to send an accused person south but only $5 to set the person free
Its Fugitive Slave Act helped inspire Harriet Beecher Stowe’s _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_ (1852)
Clay’s last great deal between North and South, after an 1820 deal over Missouri and Maine and an 1833 tariff deal; he died in 1852
Its popular sovereignty idea returned in Douglas’s Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854), which repealed the 36°30′ line
Last great Senate debate of the “Great Triumvirate”: Clay proposed it, Webster supported it, and Calhoun opposed it
The gold rush brought so many settlers that California wrote an antislavery state constitution in 1849 and skipped being a territory

trap.title: Which compromise?
trap.body: Henry Clay helped pass three famous deals: the Missouri Compromise (1820), the Compromise Tariff of 1833, and this one, so an early buzz on Clay clues can go wrong. The Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854 also used popular sovereignty, and the Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction. Some tossups ask only for one of this deal’s five laws, the Fugitive Slave Act, and then “Compromise of 1850” is wrong.
trap.fix: California, Utah and New Mexico, the slave trade in Washington, D.C., Zachary Taylor’s death, Millard Fillmore, and Webster’s Seventh of March speech mean 1850. Maine, Missouri, and the 36°30′ line mean 1820; Kansas means 1854; Rutherford B. Hayes means 1877. Saying just “compromise” earns a prompt, so give the year.
trap.line: Real answer line: Compromise of 1850 (prompt on compromise alone or Omnibus Bill; do not accept “Missouri Compromise,” “Kansas–Nebraska Act,” “Fugitive Slave Act,” or “Compromise of 1877”)

topics.name: Dawes Act
topics.kicker: Broke reservations into family plots · Native land fell by two-thirds
topics.briefing: In 1887, Congress decided to break up Native American reservations into private farms. The Dawes Act, sponsored by Senator Henry Dawes of Massachusetts, gave 160 acres to each head of a family and sold the leftover “surplus” land to white settlers. Supporters said it would help Native Americans by making them farmers, but by 1934 Native nations had lost about 90 million acres, roughly two-thirds of their land.
topics.answerHtml: Dawes Act (or Dawes Severalty Act or General Allotment Act; prompt on allotment; do not accept “Dawes Plan”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Theodore Roosevelt praised this law in 1901 as “a mighty pulverizing engine to break up the tribal mass.” Over the 47 years after this law passed, Native American landholdings shrank from about 138 million acres to about 48 million acres.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 law that divided reservation land into plots for individual Native American families.

tossups.p: John Collier, Franklin Roosevelt’s Commissioner of Indian Affairs, pushed for a 1934 law that ended the policy begun by this earlier law. That 1934 law, the Indian Reorganization Act, encouraged Native nations to write constitutions and rebuild their own governments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 law, signed by Grover Cleveland, that broke up reservations into individual plots.

tossups.p: In 1928, the Meriam Report described deep poverty on many reservations and criticized the land policy begun by this law. That report helped lead to a major change in federal policy toward Native Americans six years later.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 law that split up reservations into plots of up to 160 acres.

tossups.p: Reformers who called themselves “Friends of the Indian” and met each year at Lake Mohonk in New York backed this law. Helen Hunt Jackson’s book _A Century of Dishonor_ had earlier stirred calls to change the government’s treatment of Native peoples.
tossups.r: Supporters hoped this law would turn Native Americans into individual farmers. For 10 points, name this 1887 law that divided reservations into family plots.

tossups.p: This law gave 80 acres to each single adult and to each orphan under 18, and 40 acres to each other single person under 18. The federal government then sold off much of the reservation land left over after those plots were handed out.
tossups.r: Heads of families received 160 acres. For 10 points, name this 1887 law that broke up Native American reservations.

tossups.p: The federal government held each plot created by this law in trust for 25 years, and during that time the owner could not sell it. Native Americans who accepted plots under this law were also declared citizens of the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 law that divided reservation land among individual Native American families.

tossups.p: The government labeled the reservation land it did not hand out under this law as “surplus” and opened it to white settlers. By the 1930s, Native nations had lost about two-thirds of the land they had held before this law passed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 law, signed by Grover Cleveland, that split reservations into individual plots.

tossups.p: This law at first exempted the Cherokee, the Creek, and the rest of the “Five Civilized Tribes” in Indian Territory. Congress extended its policy to those nations with the Curtis Act of 1898, and a federal commission drew up membership rolls that those nations have used to decide citizenship.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 law that broke up Native American reservations into individual plots.

tossups.p: Because land was sold to outsiders under this law, many reservations became a “checkerboard” of Native-owned and non-Native-owned plots. Over generations, the plots created by this law were divided among so many heirs that some owners held only tiny shares.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 law that split reservation land into plots for individual families.

tossups.p: This law gave each Native American head of a family the same amount of land that a settler could claim under the Homestead Act of 1862. Much of the land handed out under this law was too dry to farm, and many owners later lost their plots to taxes, debts, or fraud.
tossups.r: That amount was 160 acres. For 10 points, name this 1887 law that divided reservations into individual plots.

tossups.p: The Massachusetts senator who sponsored this law chaired the Senate’s Committee on Indian Affairs. After leaving the Senate in 1893, he led a federal commission that pressed the “Five Civilized Tribes” to accept the policy of this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 law, named for that senator, that broke up reservations into individual plots.

tossups.p: The Burke Act of 1906 changed this law so that Native Americans who received plots became citizens only when the plot’s trust period ended, unless officials declared them “competent” sooner. Many owners who gained full control of their plots early soon lost them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 law that split Native American reservations into individual plots.

tossups.p: In 1903, the Kiowa leader Lone Wolf lost a Supreme Court case against the breakup of his people’s reservation under the policy of this law. In _Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock_, the Court ruled that Congress could override promises made in treaties.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 law that divided reservations into plots for individual Native American families.

tossups.p: Native Americans who had not gained citizenship by accepting plots under this law were made citizens by the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924. A decade later, the Indian Reorganization Act stopped any further dividing of reservations under this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 law, signed by Grover Cleveland, that broke up reservations into individual plots.

tossups.p: This law was signed just four days after the Interstate Commerce Act, which created the first federal agency to regulate railroads. A former governor of New York signed both laws in February 1887.
tossups.r: That president was Grover Cleveland. For 10 points, name this law that aimed to turn Native Americans into individual farmers by dividing up reservations.

clues.t: An 1887 law that divided (allotted) reservation land into plots for individual Native American families
Signed by President Grover Cleveland in February 1887
Aimed to turn Native Americans into individual farmers and end tribes’ holding of land in common (assimilation)
Each head of a family received 160 acres
Leftover “surplus” reservation land was sold to white settlers
Native landholdings fell from about 138 million acres (1887) to about 48 million acres (1934), a loss of about two-thirds
Each plot was held in trust by the government for 25 years and could not be sold during that time
Native Americans who accepted plots were declared U.S. citizens
Ended by the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, pushed by Commissioner of Indian Affairs John Collier
At first did not apply to the “Five Civilized Tribes” in Indian Territory; the Curtis Act (1898) extended the policy to them
Theodore Roosevelt (1901): “a mighty pulverizing engine to break up the tribal mass”
The Meriam Report (1928) described deep poverty on reservations and criticized the allotment policy
Reformers who called themselves “Friends of the Indian” supported it at their yearly Lake Mohonk conferences in New York
Helen Hunt Jackson’s _A Century of Dishonor_ (1881) had stirred calls to reform federal policy toward Native peoples
Single adults and orphans under 18 got 80 acres; other single people under 18 got 40 acres
The Burke Act (1906) delayed citizenship until a plot’s trust period ended, unless officials declared the owner “competent”
Left many reservations a “checkerboard” of Native and non-Native land; over generations, plots were split among many heirs
Its 160 acres matched a settler’s claim under the Homestead Act of 1862; much of the land was too dry to farm
_Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock_ (1903): a Kiowa leader lost, and the Court ruled Congress could override treaty promises
Its sponsor, a Massachusetts senator, chaired the Committee on Indian Affairs and later led a commission to the “Five Civilized Tribes” (from 1893)
That commission drew up membership rolls of the Five Tribes, which those nations have used to decide citizenship
Native Americans who were not yet citizens became citizens under the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924
Signed four days after the Interstate Commerce Act, which created the first federal agency to regulate railroads
Many owners later lost their plots to taxes, debts, or fraud

trap.title: Act, not Plan
trap.body: Several famous Daweses show up in history questions. Senator Henry Dawes of Massachusetts sponsored this 1887 law about Native American land, while Charles Dawes, a banker who later became Calvin Coolidge’s vice president, led the committee behind the 1924 Dawes Plan for Germany’s World War I reparations. William Dawes rode with Paul Revere in 1775. Saying “Dawes Plan” for this law is wrong, and so is the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, which ended allotment.
trap.fix: Native American land, 160-acre plots, “surplus” land sold to settlers, and 1887 mean the Dawes Act; Germany, reparations, and the 1920s mean the Dawes Plan. “Dawes” or “General Allotment Act” is fine, but “allotment” alone may earn only a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Dawes Act (or Dawes Severalty Act or General Allotment Act; prompt on allotment; do not accept “Dawes Plan”)

topics.name: Democratic-Republican Party
topics.kicker: Party of Jefferson and Madison · Rival of the Federalists, 1790s–1820s
topics.briefing: In the early 1790s, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison organized a party to fight Alexander Hamilton’s Federalists. Its members usually called themselves “Republicans,” and they wanted a small national government, a strict reading of the Constitution, and a nation of independent farmers. The Democratic-Republican Party won the presidency in 1800, and its leaders held that office for decades before the party split apart after the election of 1824.
topics.answerHtml: Democratic-Republican Party (accept Democratic-Republicans or Jeffersonian Republicans; prompt on Republicans; do not accept “Republican Party” or “Democratic Party”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The secretary of state gave the poet Philip Freneau [“freh-NOH”] a job as a State Department translator in 1791, and Freneau soon began the _National Gazette_, a newspaper that spoke for this party. That paper’s chief rival was John Fenno’s _Gazette of the United States_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this political party founded by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison to oppose Alexander Hamilton’s Federalists.

tossups.p: After a bitter campaign, the first president from this party declared in his inaugural address, “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.” Years later, he described his own victory as “the revolution of 1800.”
tossups.r: That president was Thomas Jefferson. For 10 points, name this party that he and James Madison founded to oppose the Federalists.

tossups.p: John Randolph of Roanoke led a small group called the “Tertium Quids” [“TER-shee-um KWIDZ”] that broke away from this party around 1806, accusing its leaders of abandoning the principles of limited government. Randolph had been one of this party’s leaders in the House.
tossups.r: Thomas Jefferson was then the president from this party. For 10 points, name this party that opposed the Federalists.

tossups.p: In 1800, two candidates from this party tied with 73 electoral votes each, so the House of Representatives had to choose between them, finally doing so on its 36th ballot. That tie led to the Twelfth Amendment, which had electors vote separately for president and vice president.
tossups.r: The winner was Thomas Jefferson. For 10 points, name this party that Jefferson founded with James Madison.

tossups.p: In 1820, a president from this party won every electoral vote but one, which William Plumer of New Hampshire cast for John Quincy Adams. The only other major party of the time had not even nominated a candidate against him.
tossups.r: That president, James Monroe, led the country during the Era of Good Feelings. For 10 points, name this party founded by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison.

tossups.p: This party’s members in Congress met in a caucus to pick its presidential candidates, a system critics called “King Caucus.” That system collapsed in 1824, when the caucus chose William Crawford but three other members of this party also ran for president.
tossups.r: After that election, the party split into followers of Andrew Jackson and of John Quincy Adams. For 10 points, name this party founded by Thomas Jefferson.

tossups.p: In 1798, two founders of this party secretly wrote resolutions for the legislatures of Kentucky and Virginia, arguing that states could resist unconstitutional federal laws. Those resolutions attacked the Alien and Sedition Acts, which John Adams had signed.
tossups.r: Those founders were Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. For 10 points, name the political party they created.

tossups.p: In 1816, a president from this party signed a charter for the Second Bank of the United States, even though in 1791 he had argued in the House that Congress had no power to create the first national bank. That same year, this party’s Congress passed what is often called the first protective tariff.
tossups.r: That president, James Madison, had led the country through the War of 1812. For 10 points, name the party he founded with Thomas Jefferson.

tossups.p: Members of this party condemned the treaty that John Jay signed with Britain in 1794, and protesters burned Jay in effigy. In 1796, this party’s leaders in the House of Representatives tried, and failed, to block the money needed to carry out that treaty.
tossups.r: This party generally favored France over Britain. For 10 points, name this party led by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison.

tossups.p: In a 1791 opinion for George Washington, a future founder of this party argued that Congress had no power to charter a national bank, because the Constitution did not list that power. The treasury secretary answered that the Constitution’s “necessary and proper” clause implied such powers.
tossups.r: This party, which opposed Alexander Hamilton’s Federalists, favored a strict reading of the Constitution. For 10 points, name this party founded by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison.

tossups.p: Swiss-born Albert Gallatin [“GAL-uh-tin”], a leader of this party in the House, later served as Treasury Secretary longer than anyone else in history, cutting the national debt under two of its presidents. Gallatin also helped negotiate the Treaty of Ghent.
tossups.r: Those presidents were Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. For 10 points, name the party they founded.

tossups.p: In a November 1794 speech to Congress, George Washington blamed “self-created societies” for stirring up the Whiskey Rebellion, meaning political clubs that shared this party’s views. Many of those clubs had been inspired by the French Revolution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this party founded by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison to oppose Hamilton’s Federalists.

tossups.p: A president from this party worried that the Constitution did not allow him to buy land from a foreign country, so he drafted an amendment to permit it. He went ahead with the purchase anyway in 1803, roughly doubling the size of the country.
tossups.r: That president, Thomas Jefferson, made the Louisiana Purchase. For 10 points, name the party he founded with James Madison.

tossups.p: Young members of this party called “War Hawks,” led by Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun, pushed Congress to declare war on Britain in 1812. The rival party’s opposition to that war, shown at the Hartford Convention, helped leave this party with almost no opponents.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this party of Thomas Jefferson, James Madison, and James Monroe.

tossups.p: Critics drew a snapping turtle named “Ograbme” [“oh-GRAB-mee”] to mock a law passed by this party, since the turtle’s name spelled “embargo” backward. That 1807 law banned American ships from trading at foreign ports and badly hurt New England’s merchants.
tossups.r: That law was signed by Thomas Jefferson. For 10 points, name the party Jefferson founded with James Madison.

clues.t: Founded by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison in the early 1790s
Rival of Alexander Hamilton’s Federalist Party; together they made up the first U.S. two-party system
Its presidents: Jefferson, Madison, James Monroe, and John Quincy Adams
Favored a strict reading of the Constitution, states’ rights, a small national government, and farmers
Won the presidency in the election of 1800, which Jefferson called “the revolution of 1800”
Ruled almost unopposed during James Monroe’s “Era of Good Feelings” (1817–1825)
Split after the election of 1824: Andrew Jackson’s followers became the Democrats, and Adams and Clay’s became the National Republicans
Jefferson and Madison secretly wrote the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions (1798) against the Alien and Sedition Acts
Opposed John Jay’s 1794 treaty with Britain and generally favored France
Jefferson argued in a 1791 opinion that Hamilton’s national bank was unconstitutional
Members usually called it the “Republican” party, but it is not the modern Republican Party, founded in 1854
Jefferson’s First Inaugural Address (1801): “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists”
Philip Freneau’s _National Gazette_ (1791), backed by Jefferson, spoke for it; John Fenno’s _Gazette of the United States_ backed Hamilton
John Randolph of Roanoke led the “Tertium Quids,” a small group that broke away around 1806
In 1800, Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied with 73 electoral votes; the House chose Jefferson on its 36th ballot, leading to the 12th Amendment
In 1820, Monroe won every electoral vote but one, cast by William Plumer for John Quincy Adams
Its members of Congress picked its presidential nominees in a caucus (“King Caucus”) until 1824, when they chose William Crawford
Under Madison, it chartered the Second Bank of the United States and passed a protective tariff (both 1816), though Madison had opposed the first bank in 1791
Albert Gallatin, the longest-serving Treasury Secretary, cut the national debt under Jefferson and Madison
Washington blamed clubs that shared its views, the “self-created societies,” for the Whiskey Rebellion (1794)
Jefferson doubted the Constitution allowed the Louisiana Purchase (1803) and drafted an amendment, but went ahead anyway
Its “War Hawks,” led by Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun, pushed for the War of 1812; the Federalists’ Hartford Convention opposed that war
Jefferson’s Embargo Act (1807) hurt New England; critics drew a snapping turtle named “Ograbme” (embargo spelled backward)
Protesters burned John Jay in effigy; in 1796, its House leaders failed to block money to carry out his treaty

trap.title: Neither modern party
trap.body: This party’s members usually called themselves “Republicans,” but it is not the Republican Party of Abraham Lincoln, which was founded in 1854. The modern Democratic Party grew out of Andrew Jackson’s wing of this party in the late 1820s, but it is a separate answer line too. Real answer lines prompt on “Republicans” and do not accept “Republican Party” or “Democratic Party.”
trap.fix: Use the date: clues from the 1790s to the 1820s, like Jefferson, Madison, Monroe, and fights with the Federalists, want the Democratic-Republicans. Say the full name, “Democratic-Republican Party,” so you are not stuck with a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Democratic-Republican Party (accept Jeffersonian Republicans; prompt on Republicans; do not accept “Republican Party” or “Democratic Party”)

topics.name: Denali
topics.kicker: Tallest mountain in North America · Alaska’s “high one,” 20,310 feet
topics.briefing: Denali, in Alaska, is the tallest mountain in North America at 20,310 feet, and its name comes from a Koyukon Athabaskan word meaning “the high one.” In 1913, Walter Harper, a young Alaska Native man, became the first person to stand on its summit. The federal government called it Mount McKinley until 2015, when it officially became Denali, and a 2025 executive order restored “Mount McKinley” for federal use.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On June 7, 1913, Walter Harper became the first person to stand on this mountain’s summit. He climbed with Harry Karstens, Robert Tatum, and Hudson Stuck, an Episcopal archdeacon who later wrote a book about their climb.
tossups.r: Harper was a young Alaska Native man. For 10 points, name this mountain, the tallest peak in North America.

tossups.p: In 1906, Frederick Cook claimed to have made the first climb of this mountain, but his “summit” photograph was later shown to have been taken on a much smaller peak miles away. Two years later, Cook made another disputed claim, that he had reached the North Pole.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mountain in Alaska, the highest point in North America.

tossups.p: In 1910, four gold miners from Fairbanks set out to climb this mountain, and two of them reached its lower North Peak, where they planted a tall spruce pole. Climbers who reached the higher South Peak three years later said they could see the pole.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this peak in the Alaska Range, the highest mountain in North America.

tossups.p: The name that this mountain’s Koyukon Athabaskan [“ath-uh-BASS-kun”] neighbors gave it means “the high one.” Its state government adopted that name for the mountain in 1975, but federal maps kept using a name chosen by a gold prospector.
tossups.r: The federal government switched to the Native name in 2015. For 10 points, name this mountain, the tallest in North America.

tossups.p: For decades, members of Congress from Ohio blocked efforts to change this mountain’s official name. In 1980, Congress renamed and greatly enlarged the national park around it, which had been created in 1917.
tossups.r: The mountain itself got a new official name in 2015. For 10 points, name this mountain in Alaska, the tallest in North America.

tossups.p: In 1951, Bradford Washburn led the first climb of this mountain by its West Buttress, which became its most popular route. Four years earlier, his wife, Barbara Washburn, had become the first woman to reach its summit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mountain in the Alaska Range, the highest point in North America.

tossups.p: Most climbers of this mountain fly in small planes from the town of Talkeetna [“tal-KEET-nuh”] to a base camp on the Kahiltna [“kuh-HILT-nuh”] Glacier. From there, most expeditions spend weeks working their way up to its summit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mountain in the Alaska Range, the tallest peak in North America.

tossups.p: This mountain rises about 18,000 feet from its base, a bigger rise than Mount Everest’s from the high plateau around it. Only Everest and Aconcagua [“ah-kon-KAH-gwuh”] stand out more from their surroundings, a measure called prominence.
tossups.r: It is one of the “Seven Summits,” the highest peaks on each continent. For 10 points, name this mountain, the highest in North America.

tossups.p: The photographer Ansel Adams took famous pictures of this mountain from Wonder Lake in 1947. Visitors to the national park around it hope to spot its “Big Five” animals: grizzly bears, moose, caribou, wolves, and Dall sheep.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mountain in Alaska, the tallest in North America.

tossups.p: The naturalist Charles Sheldon campaigned for a national park around this mountain to protect its Dall sheep from market hunters. Congress created that park in 1917, and Harry Karstens, who had climbed this mountain, later became its first superintendent.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mountain, the highest peak in North America.

tossups.p: A long fault named for this mountain slipped in a magnitude 7.9 earthquake in 2002. A major oil pipeline that crosses the fault survived that earthquake because engineers had set it on sliding supports, letting the ground shift beneath it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mountain in the Alaska Range, the tallest in North America.

tossups.p: Hudson Stuck, who organized the first successful climb of this mountain, used its Native name in the title of his 1914 book about that climb. Stuck argued that the name prospectors had given this mountain should be dropped.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alaskan mountain, the tallest peak in North America.

tossups.p: In 1896, a gold prospector named William Dickey renamed this mountain to honor a presidential candidate who supported the gold standard. In 1917, Congress gave that name to the new national park around this mountain.
tossups.r: That candidate later became the 25th president. For 10 points, name this mountain, the highest in North America.

tossups.p: Because it lies at about 63 degrees north latitude, this mountain is one of the coldest big peaks on Earth, and the air pressure near its summit is lower than on peaks of similar height nearer the equator. Its national park covers about six million acres.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this peak in the Alaska Range, the tallest mountain in North America.

tossups.p: A 2015 survey using GPS equipment lowered this mountain’s official height by ten feet, from the figure of 20,320 feet that had been used for decades. Survey teams carried their instruments all the way to its summit.
tossups.r: That survey set its official height at 20,310 feet. For 10 points, name this mountain, the tallest in North America, first climbed in 1913.

clues.t: The tallest mountain in North America, at 20,310 feet
In the Alaska Range in south-central Alaska
Officially given its Native name in 2015; a 2025 executive order restored the 25th president’s name for federal use
Centerpiece of a national park created in 1917 and renamed and enlarged in 1980
Its name comes from a Koyukon Athabaskan word meaning “the high one”
First climbed on June 7, 1913; Walter Harper, a young Alaska Native man, was the first to reach the top
Hudson Stuck, an Episcopal archdeacon, organized the 1913 climb with Harry Karstens and Robert Tatum
Frederick Cook falsely claimed the first climb in 1906
Gold prospector William Dickey renamed it in 1896 for a presidential candidate who backed the gold standard (the future 25th president)
One of the “Seven Summits,” the highest peaks on each of the seven continents
Alaska adopted its Native name in 1975, but Ohio’s members of Congress blocked a federal change for decades
1910: four miners from Fairbanks (the “Sourdoughs”) tried it; two reached the lower North Peak and planted a spruce pole
Cook’s “summit” photo was taken on a much smaller peak miles away; he later made a disputed North Pole claim (1908)
Bradford Washburn led the first climb by the West Buttress (1951), which became the most popular route
Barbara Washburn was the first woman to reach the summit (1947)
Climbers fly from Talkeetna to a base camp on the Kahiltna Glacier
Rises about 18,000 feet from its base, more than Everest’s rise from its high plateau; third in prominence after Everest and Aconcagua
Naturalist Charles Sheldon pushed for its national park to protect Dall sheep; climber Harry Karstens became the park’s first superintendent
Ansel Adams photographed it from Wonder Lake (1947); the park’s “Big Five” are grizzlies, moose, caribou, wolves, and Dall sheep
The fault named for it slipped in a magnitude 7.9 earthquake (2002); the Trans-Alaska Pipeline survived on sliding supports
Hudson Stuck used its Native name in the title of his 1914 book about the first climb
At about 63° north, it is one of the coldest big mountains, with lower air pressure than peaks nearer the equator
A 2015 GPS survey set its height at 20,310 feet, ten feet lower than the old figure of 20,320

trap.title: Mountain or president?
trap.body: This mountain has two names, and both count: Denali, from its Koyukon name, and Mount McKinley, after the 25th president. The federal government officially renamed it Denali in 2015, and a 2025 executive order restored “Mount McKinley” for federal use, so tossups may use either name. Saying just “McKinley” earns a prompt, and naming the president himself on a mountain question is wrong.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this mountain” or “this peak,” say “Denali” or “Mount McKinley.” If it asks for “this president,” the answer is William McKinley. Don’t mix it up with Mount Logan, the tallest peak in Canada, or Mount Whitney, the tallest in the lower 48 states.
trap.line: Real answer line: Denali (or Mount McKinley; prompt on McKinley)

topics.name: Department of Education
topics.kicker: Cabinet department for schools and student aid · Created under Carter, 1979
topics.briefing: Most American public schools are run by states and local school boards, but the U.S. Department of Education oversees federal money for schools and colleges. Jimmy Carter signed the law creating it in 1979, splitting it off from a bigger department, and it opened in 1980 with Shirley Hufstedler, a federal judge, as its first secretary. It runs Pell Grants and the FAFSA, the form students fill out to get help paying for college.
topics.answerHtml: Department of Education (accept Education Department; prompt on education; do not accept “Department of Energy” or “Department of Health, Education, and Welfare”)
reject: department of health education and welfare
department of health and human services
department of housing and urban development

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A federal appeals court judge, Shirley Hufstedler [“HUFF-sted-ler”], became the first person to lead this executive department. She served until early 1981, when Terrel Bell, Ronald Reagan’s choice for the job, took over.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, created under Jimmy Carter, that oversees federal school programs and student aid.

tossups.p: Henry Barnard, a school reformer from Connecticut, was the first commissioner of an 1867 federal agency that was this department’s forerunner. Congressman James Garfield had sponsored the law creating that agency, which was demoted to an office just a year later.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, created in 1979 under Jimmy Carter.

tossups.p: This department runs grants named for Senator Claiborne Pell of Rhode Island, which help students from low-income families pay for college. To apply for that aid, students fill out a form called the FAFSA, short for Free Application for Federal Student Aid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, created under Jimmy Carter, that oversees federal school programs.

tossups.p: This department was carved out of a larger department created in 1953, whose first secretary, Oveta Culp Hobby, was only the second woman ever to serve in a president’s Cabinet. The rest of that older department was renamed Health and Human Services.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this department that opened in 1980, a year after Jimmy Carter signed the law creating it.

tossups.p: This department carries out IDEA, a law guaranteeing children with disabilities a free public school program suited to their needs. Gerald Ford signed the first version of that law in 1975, and Congress gave it the name IDEA in 1990.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, created in 1979, which also runs federal student aid.

tossups.p: In 1983, a commission formed by this department’s second leader, Terrel Bell, warned of “a rising tide of mediocrity” in American schools. That commission’s report, _A Nation at Risk_, set off decades of efforts to raise school standards.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, first led by Shirley Hufstedler.

tossups.p: Lauro Cavazos [“kuh-VAH-sohs”], who took charge of this department in 1988, was the first Hispanic American to serve in a president’s Cabinet. In 2001, Rod Paige, a former Houston schools superintendent, became the first African American to lead this department.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, created by Jimmy Carter, that runs federal student aid.

tossups.p: In 2002, George W. Bush signed No Child Left Behind, which required states to test students every year in reading and math, and this department enforced it. In 2015, Barack Obama signed the Every Student Succeeds Act, which replaced that law and gave states more control.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, created in 1979, that oversees federal school programs.

tossups.p: This department’s Office for Civil Rights enforces Title IX, a 1972 law that bans discrimination based on sex in school programs that receive federal money. That law helped bring about a large increase in girls’ and women’s sports.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, first led by Shirley Hufstedler in 1979.

tossups.p: This department runs Title I, which sends money to schools serving many children from low-income families. That program began with a 1965 law that Lyndon Johnson signed outside the one-room schoolhouse in Texas where he had started school as a boy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, created under Jimmy Carter, that also runs federal student aid.

tossups.p: In 2017, Vice President Mike Pence cast the first tie-breaking vote ever needed to confirm a Cabinet secretary, making Betsy DeVos the head of this department. DeVos, a businesswoman from Michigan, held that job until January 2021.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, created in 1979, whose first leader was Shirley Hufstedler.

tossups.p: The nation’s largest teachers’ union endorsed a presidential candidate for the first time in 1976, partly because he promised to create this department. The bill creating it later passed the House of Representatives by a narrow margin.
tossups.r: That candidate, Jimmy Carter, signed the bill in 1979. For 10 points, name this department, which opened in 1980.

tossups.p: Arne Duncan, who had run Chicago’s public schools, led this department under Barack Obama. Duncan ran Race to the Top, a contest in which states competed for billions of dollars in grants by promising to change their schools.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, first led by Shirley Hufstedler.

tossups.p: In his 1980 campaign, Ronald Reagan promised to abolish this new department, and debates over whether to keep it have returned in later decades. Once in office, Reagan instead appointed three men to lead it in turn: Terrel Bell, William Bennett, and Lauro Cavazos.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, created under Jimmy Carter in 1979.

tossups.p: William Bennett, who led this department in the late 1980s, later became the first director of the White House office that coordinates national drug-control policy. Bennett also edited _The Book of Virtues_, a 1993 collection of stories meant to teach good character.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Cabinet department, created in 1979 under Jimmy Carter, that runs federal student aid.

clues.t: Created by a law Jimmy Carter signed in October 1979
Began operating in May 1980
Cabinet department that oversees federal programs for schools and federal student aid for college
First secretary (1979–1981): Shirley Hufstedler, who had been a federal appeals court judge
Split off from an older department called HEW (created 1953); the rest of HEW became Health and Human Services
Runs Pell Grants (named for Senator Claiborne Pell) and the FAFSA, the Free Application for Federal Student Aid
Carries out IDEA, the law guaranteeing children with disabilities a free public school program suited to their needs
Its Office for Civil Rights enforces Title IX (1972), which bans sex discrimination in school programs that get federal money
Enforced No Child Left Behind (2002, George W. Bush), which was replaced by the Every Student Succeeds Act (2015, Barack Obama)
Its forerunner, an 1867 federal agency, was first led by Commissioner Henry Barnard and was demoted to an office a year later
_A Nation at Risk_ (1983), from a commission formed by Secretary Terrel Bell, warned of “a rising tide of mediocrity”
A March 2025 executive order directed steps toward closing it; fully abolishing it would take an act of Congress
Congressman James Garfield sponsored the 1867 law that created its forerunner
Oveta Culp Hobby, the first head of HEW (1953), was the second woman in a president’s Cabinet
Gerald Ford signed the 1975 law that was renamed IDEA in 1990
Lauro Cavazos (from 1988) was the first Hispanic American in a president’s Cabinet
Rod Paige, a former Houston schools superintendent, became its first African American secretary (2001)
Runs Title I, money for schools serving many low-income children, which began with a 1965 law Lyndon Johnson signed at his boyhood one-room schoolhouse
In 2017, Vice President Mike Pence cast the first tie-breaking vote ever needed to confirm a Cabinet secretary, Betsy DeVos
The nation’s largest teachers’ union made its first presidential endorsement, for Carter, in 1976, partly over his promise to create it
Arne Duncan, Barack Obama’s secretary, ran Race to the Top, a contest for billions of dollars in state grants
Ronald Reagan’s three secretaries: Terrel Bell, William Bennett, and Lauro Cavazos
William Bennett later became the first director of national drug-control policy and edited _The Book of Virtues_ (1993)

trap.title: Education or Energy?
trap.body: Jimmy Carter created two Cabinet departments: the Department of Energy in 1977 and this one in 1979, so the president clue alone won’t tell you which. This department also grew out of an older one, Health, Education, and Welfare (1953), whose leftover parts became Health and Human Services. Don’t answer the older U.S. Office of Education, which this department replaced in 1980, or the court case _Brown v. Board of Education_.
trap.fix: Oil, nuclear power, and the 1970s energy crisis mean Energy, which is usually called “DOE.” Schools, Pell Grants, the FAFSA, Title IX, and Shirley Hufstedler mean this department, whose official abbreviation is “ED.” Say the whole name, because “education” alone may only earn a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Department of Education (accept Education Department; prompt on education; do not accept “Department of Energy” or “Department of Health, Education, and Welfare”)

topics.name: DeWitt Clinton
topics.kicker: New York governor and New York City mayor · Father of the Erie Canal
topics.briefing: When DeWitt Clinton pushed to dig a canal more than 360 miles across New York, from the Hudson River to Lake Erie, critics laughed and called it “Clinton’s Ditch.” As governor, he got it built anyway, and in 1825 he celebrated its opening by pouring a keg of Lake Erie water into the Atlantic Ocean. Earlier, he had served as mayor of New York City and run for president against James Madison.
topics.answerHtml: DeWitt Clinton (prompt on Clinton; do not accept “George Clinton,” “Bill Clinton,” “Erie Canal,” or “Clinton’s Ditch”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Martin Van Buren led a faction called the Bucktails, named for the deer tails its members wore on their hats, against this man’s followers. In 1824, this man’s enemies in the legislature removed him from a state board he had served on for years, but voters were so angry that they elected him governor that fall.
tossups.r: That board oversaw the building of the Erie Canal. For 10 points, name this New York politician.

tossups.p: In November 1825, after riding the boat _Seneca Chief_ from Buffalo to New York City, this man poured a keg of lake water into the Atlantic Ocean. People called that ceremony the “Wedding of the Waters.”
tossups.r: The water came from Lake Erie, and the ceremony celebrated the opening of the Erie Canal. For 10 points, name this New York governor.

tossups.p: In 1812, Federalist leaders meeting secretly in New York City agreed to back this Democratic-Republican for president instead of naming a candidate of their own. His running mate in that race was Jared Ingersoll of Pennsylvania.
tossups.r: This man lost to James Madison. For 10 points, name this New Yorker who later championed the Erie Canal as governor.

tossups.p: This man served as mayor of New York City for most of the years from 1803 to 1815, and for part of that time he was also the state’s lieutenant governor. He had resigned from the U.S. Senate to take the mayor’s job.
tossups.r: As governor, he later pushed through the Erie Canal. For 10 points, name this New York politician.

tossups.p: In 1805, this man helped found the Free School Society, which opened free schools for poor children in New York City. He became the society’s president while he was also serving as the city’s mayor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man, later the governor of New York who championed the Erie Canal.

tossups.p: An early steam locomotive named for this man pulled one of the first passenger trains in New York State, on the Mohawk and Hudson Railroad between Albany and Schenectady [“skuh-NEK-tuh-dee”] in 1831. This man had died three years earlier.
tossups.r: He had been governor of New York when the Erie Canal opened. For 10 points, name this politician.

tossups.p: On July 4, 1817, just days after this man took office, workers broke ground at Rome, New York, on a project he had championed for years. Critics mocked that project as his “Big Ditch” and his “Folly.”
tossups.r: That project was the Erie Canal. For 10 points, name this New York governor.

tossups.p: After graduating from Columbia College in 1786, this man became private secretary to his uncle, who was New York’s first governor and later served as vice president under Thomas Jefferson and James Madison.
tossups.r: That uncle was George Clinton. For 10 points, name this nephew, the New York governor who championed the Erie Canal.

tossups.p: In 1802, this man fought a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey, with John Swartwout, a friend and ally of Aaron Burr. Swartwout was wounded, but both men survived, and this man left the U.S. Senate the next year to become a mayor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Yorker who later championed the Erie Canal as governor.

tossups.p: In 1820, this man narrowly won reelection by defeating Daniel Tompkins, who was then serving as vice president of the United States. This man did not run again in 1822, but he won back his office two years later.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this governor of New York who championed the Erie Canal.

tossups.p: A fort at the southern tip of Manhattan, built just before the War of 1812, was renamed in 1815 to honor this man, the city’s longtime mayor. As Castle Garden, that fort later served as New York’s main station for arriving immigrants before Ellis Island opened.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mayor and governor who championed the Erie Canal.

tossups.p: In one presidential election, this candidate carried every New England state except Vermont, along with New York, New Jersey, and Delaware, but he lost the electoral vote 128 to 89.
tossups.r: He lost that 1812 race to James Madison. For 10 points, name this New Yorker who later championed the Erie Canal.

tossups.p: In 1810, this man and Gouverneur Morris were named to a state commission that traveled across western New York to study a possible route for a waterway. Years later, this man led the effort to build it.
tossups.r: That waterway became the Erie Canal. For 10 points, name this mayor of New York City and governor of New York.

tossups.p: After this man died suddenly in office in February 1828, his longtime rival Martin Van Buren won the election to replace him. Van Buren served only about ten weeks before leaving to become Andrew Jackson’s secretary of state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York governor who championed the Erie Canal.

tossups.p: Months before this man ran for president in 1812, his uncle died in office as vice president, the first vice president ever to do so. That uncle had also served as New York’s first governor.
tossups.r: That uncle was George Clinton. For 10 points, name this nephew, who later championed the Erie Canal as governor.

clues.t: Championed the Erie Canal, a waterway of more than 360 miles across New York State
The canal opened in 1825, linking the Hudson River at Albany with Lake Erie at Buffalo
Governor of New York (1817–1822 and 1825–1828)
Critics mocked the canal as his “Ditch,” his “Big Ditch,” or his “Folly”
“Wedding of the Waters” (1825): rode the _Seneca Chief_ to New York City and poured a keg of Lake Erie water into the Atlantic
Mayor of New York City for most of the years from 1803 to 1815
Lost the 1812 presidential election to James Madison, 128 electoral votes to 89
Nephew of George Clinton, New York’s first governor and vice president under Jefferson and Madison
In 1812, Federalists backed him, a Democratic-Republican, as did Republicans who opposed the War of 1812
Martin Van Buren’s faction, the Bucktails, led the opposition to his followers in New York
His enemies removed him from the canal commission in 1824; the backlash helped him win back the governorship that year
Helped found the Free School Society (1805), which opened free schools for poor children in New York City
An early steam locomotive named for him ran on the Mohawk and Hudson Railroad (1831)
Ground was broken for the canal at Rome, New York, on July 4, 1817, days after he took office
Graduated from Columbia College (1786), then became private secretary to his uncle, the governor
Fought a duel with John Swartwout, an ally of Aaron Burr, at Weehawken (1802); both men survived

trap.title: Which Clinton?
trap.body: Several famous Clintons show up in quiz bowl: DeWitt Clinton, the governor behind the Erie Canal; his uncle George Clinton, New York’s first governor and a vice president; Bill Clinton, the 42nd president; Hillary Clinton, a senator from New York (2001–2009) and secretary of state (2009–2013); and Henry Clinton, a British general in the American Revolution. Saying only “Clinton” earns a prompt. Erie Canal clues also lead tossups on the canal itself, where “Clinton’s Ditch” is accepted.
trap.fix: The Erie Canal, the Wedding of the Waters, New York City’s mayor, and the 1812 race against Madison mean DeWitt; New York’s first governor and Jefferson’s vice president mean George. Listen for the noun: “this man” or “this governor” wants “DeWitt Clinton,” while “this canal” wants the Erie Canal.
trap.line: Real answer line: DeWitt Clinton (prompt on Clinton; do not accept “George Clinton” or “Erie Canal”)

topics.name: Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell
topics.kicker: Military policy on gay service members · In force from 1994 to 2011
topics.briefing: For decades, the U.S. military did not allow gay people to serve. In 1993, President Bill Clinton and Congress settled on a compromise called Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell: officials were not to ask service members about their sexual orientation, and gay, lesbian, and bisexual troops could serve only if they kept it private. Barack Obama signed a law repealing the policy in 2010, and it officially ended on September 20, 2011.
topics.answerHtml: Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell (or DADT; prompt on Don’t Ask; do not accept “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell Repeal Act”)
accept: the dont ask dont tell policy
do not ask do not tell
reject: dont ask dont tell repeal act
dont ask dont tell repeal act of 2010
repeal of dont ask dont tell

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Northwestern University sociologist Charles Moskos is often credited with designing this policy, which took effect in 1994. It replaced a 1982 Defense Department rule that barred gay people from serving in the armed forces at all.
tossups.r: Under this policy, gay, lesbian, and bisexual troops could serve only if they kept their sexual orientation private. For 10 points, name this policy adopted under Bill Clinton.

tossups.p: Senator Sam Nunn of Georgia, who chaired the Senate Armed Services Committee, and General Colin Powell, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, opposed a new president’s plan to let gay Americans serve openly in the military. This policy was the compromise that followed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1993 policy, under which gay service members could serve if they did not reveal their sexual orientation.

tossups.p: In 2010, federal judge Virginia Phillips ruled in a lawsuit brought by the Log Cabin Republicans that this policy was unconstitutional, and she ordered the military to stop enforcing it. An appeals court soon put her order on hold.
tossups.r: Congress repealed this policy later that year. For 10 points, name this policy on gay, lesbian, and bisexual service members, adopted in 1993.

tossups.p: In November 2010, a Pentagon study led by Jeh Johnson and General Carter Ham reported on surveys of service members and their families about this policy. The study concluded that ending this policy posed a low risk to the military’s effectiveness, though troops in combat units voiced more concern.
tossups.r: Weeks later, Barack Obama signed a law repealing it. For 10 points, name this 1993 policy on gay service members.

tossups.p: In July 2011, the president, Defense Secretary Leon Panetta, and Admiral Mike Mullen certified that the armed forces were ready for this policy to end. Sixty days later, on September 20, 2011, it officially ended.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this policy, adopted under Bill Clinton, that let gay service members serve only if they kept their sexual orientation private.

tossups.p: Senator Joe Lieberman of Connecticut led a December 2010 push to end this policy, and the Senate approved its repeal by a vote of 65 to 31, with votes from both parties. Four days later, the repeal was signed into law.
tossups.r: Barack Obama signed that repeal. For 10 points, name this policy on gay service members that began under Bill Clinton.

tossups.p: By most estimates, more than 13,000 service members were discharged under this policy during the roughly 17 years it was in force. Those discharged included some who worked as Arabic translators.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this policy, adopted in 1993, that barred gay, lesbian, and bisexual troops from serving openly.

tossups.p: In February 2010, Admiral Mike Mullen, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told Congress that he personally supported ending this policy, while some other military leaders urged Congress to wait for a Pentagon study first.
tossups.r: Congress repealed this policy that December. For 10 points, name this 1993 policy on gay, lesbian, and bisexual service members.

tossups.p: During his 1992 campaign, a future president promised to end the military’s ban on gay service members, but after months of debate in 1993, he accepted this policy as a compromise instead.
tossups.r: That president was Bill Clinton. For 10 points, name this policy, under which gay troops could serve only if they did not reveal their sexual orientation.

tossups.p: Because this policy was written into a federal law in 1993, ending it took a new act of Congress rather than just an order from the president. That 1993 law also authorized the Defense Department’s spending for the coming year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this policy, which kept gay service members from serving openly until 2011.

tossups.p: In his January 2010 State of the Union address, the president promised to work with Congress that year to end this policy. Soon afterward, Defense Secretary Robert Gates ordered a study of how the military could carry out that change.
tossups.r: That president, Barack Obama, signed the repeal in December 2010. For 10 points, name this policy adopted under Bill Clinton.

tossups.p: Pennsylvania congressman Patrick Murphy, an Iraq War veteran, led the effort in the House of Representatives to end this policy. In December 2010, the House passed a repeal bill by a vote of 250 to 175.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this policy on gay, lesbian, and bisexual service members that took effect in 1994.

tossups.p: In September 2010, an effort to end this policy as part of the yearly defense bill stalled in the Senate. That December, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid brought a separate repeal bill to a vote, and it passed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this policy, adopted in 1993, that let gay service members serve only if they kept their sexual orientation private.

tossups.p: Defense Secretary Les Aspin, a former congressman from Wisconsin, issued the first guidelines for this policy in July 1993, after months of hearings in Congress about who could serve in the military.
tossups.r: Bill Clinton had announced the policy that month. For 10 points, name this policy, under which gay service members could serve only if they did not reveal their sexual orientation.

tossups.p: Massachusetts congressman Marty Meehan introduced the Military Readiness Enhancement Act in 2005 to end this policy, but that bill did not pass. Five years later, a different repeal effort succeeded.
tossups.r: Congress ended this policy in 2010. For 10 points, name this 1993 policy on gay, lesbian, and bisexual service members.

trap.title: Policy, not the repeal
trap.body: This answer line is the 1993 policy itself. The Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell Repeal Act is the 2010 law that ended it, so a question asking for “this law” signed by Barack Obama may want the repeal instead. Players also mix it up with the Defense of Marriage Act, a 1996 law about marriage that Bill Clinton also signed, and with the Supreme Court’s 2015 same-sex marriage case, _Obergefell v. Hodges_.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this policy” about who could serve openly in the military, say “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell.” If it asks for the 2010 law that ended that policy, name the repeal act. Clues about marriage point to the Defense of Marriage Act or _Obergefell_, not this policy.
trap.line: Real answer line: Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell (or DADT; do not accept “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell Repeal Act”)
